- Dense, spiky fungal sporulation — branched conidiophores with spores
- Gray-brown filamentous structures
- A dark/black mass in the upper right (possibly sclerotium)
- Characteristic fuzzy fungal growth on stem/branch tissue

This strongly suggests Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea) or possibly Sclerotinia. Let me view reference images across 4 classes.

**Analysis:**

**Test image**: Macro close-up of dense, spiky, branched fungal sporulation on plant tissue. Structures are gray-brown conidiophores with spores. Dark/black mass visible upper right (possible sclerotium). Photographer: Bruce Watt (Bugwood #5505965).

**Reference comparisons:**
- **Gray Mold (Bugwood_15)**: Microscopic Botrytis conidiophores — same branched, spore-bearing structure as test image. Strong match.
- **Gray Mold (Bugwood_21)**: Gray fuzzy growth on tomato fruit — same pathogen, different presentation.
- **Sclerotinia (Bugwood_14)**: White cottony mycelium with hard sclerotia — clearly different, no spiky sporulation.
- **Powdery Mildew (CDDM_1006)**: White powder on green leaves — completely different appearance.

The test image shows classic Botrytis cinerea sporulation: dense branched conidiophores with conidia masses in gray-brown tone on stem tissue, with a possible sclerotium in upper right. This is the hallmark macro appearance of Gray Mold.
